name: TB (Tuberculosis)
tagline: Coughing for 2+ weeks? Test today — treatment is free.

urgent.heading: Urgent — see a clinic this week
urgent.primary_message: Coughing for more than 2 weeks, coughing up blood, severe night sweats, or rapid weight loss — get to a clinic. Testing is free.
red_flags: Cough lasting more than 2 weeks — productive or dry
Coughing up blood, even small amounts
Drenching night sweats for more than a week
Chest pain that worsens with breathing
Children with persistent cough and failure to thrive

what_is_it.heading: TB in plain terms
what_is_it.lede: Tuberculosis is a bacterial infection caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis. It usually attacks the lungs but can affect any part of the body — bones, brain, kidneys, lymph nodes.
paragraphs: TB spreads through the air when an infected person coughs or sneezes. Most people exposed do not get sick straight away — the bacteria can stay dormant for years (latent TB) before becoming active. About 1 in 10 latent infections become active disease in a lifetime.

TB is curable. The standard treatment is 6 months of daily tablets — completely free at every South African clinic. The biggest danger is stopping treatment early when you feel better. Partial treatment breeds drug-resistant TB, which is far harder and longer to treat.

items.body: New TB cases in South Africa every year. One of the highest rates in the world.

items.headline: 100% free
items.body: Every test, every tablet, every visit. Drug-resistant TB treatment is also free. No medical aid needed.

items.headline: Curable
items.body: 6 months of daily medication cures standard TB completely. Drug-resistant TB takes longer but is also curable.

items.headline: HIV doubles risk
items.body: TB is the leading cause of death in people living with HIV. If you are HIV positive, get screened for TB at every visit.

pull_quote.text: Stopping TB tablets when you feel better is the most dangerous thing you can do — to yourself and to everyone around you. Drug-resistant TB starts the day someone stops their treatment.

signs.heading: What to watch for
signs.lede: TB usually develops slowly. The classic sign is a cough that just will not go away. Any cough lasting more than 2 weeks deserves a test.

items.title: Persistent cough
items.description: A cough lasting more than 2 weeks, often productive, sometimes with blood. May be worse at night.

items.title: Night sweats and fever
items.description: Drenching night sweats that soak the sheets. Low-grade fever, especially in the afternoon and evening.

items.title: Weight loss and fatigue
items.description: Unintentional weight loss over weeks or months. Loss of appetite. Tiredness out of proportion to activity.

items.title: In children
items.description: Failure to thrive, poor weight gain, persistent cough, swollen glands in the neck. TB in children is often missed — ask if a close relative has TB.

spreads.heading: How TB spreads — and how it doesn't
yes: Breathing in droplets from someone with active lung TB who is coughing or sneezing
Prolonged close contact in enclosed, poorly ventilated spaces
Living or working in crowded conditions — homes, hostels, mines, prisons
Drinking unpasteurised milk from infected cattle (rare in SA)
no: Casual contact like shaking hands or being in the same outdoor space
Sharing food, drinks, plates, or cutlery
Toilet seats, doorknobs, or bedding (once aired)

prevention.heading: How to protect yourself and your family
prevention.lede: TB thrives in poorly ventilated, crowded spaces. Most prevention is about air, early detection, and completing treatment — yours or a household contact's.

items.title: BCG vaccine at birth
items.description: Every SA baby gets a BCG injection at birth. It does not prevent all TB but reduces severe forms in children, especially meningitis.

items.title: Open windows
items.description: TB bacteria die quickly in fresh air and sunlight. Open windows, especially in bedrooms shared with someone being treated for TB.

items.title: Test household contacts
items.description: If someone in your home is diagnosed, everyone in the house should be tested — even if they feel well. Children especially need protection.

items.title: TB preventive therapy
items.description: People living with HIV, household contacts, and other at-risk groups can be given a course of TB tablets to prevent active disease. Ask at your clinic.

items.title: If you have had a cough for 2 weeks — get tested
items.description: Walk into any clinic. Ask for a TB test. You will be asked to cough up sputum into a small cup. Results within a few days.

items.title: If positive — start treatment immediately
items.description: The clinic will give you the tablets that same day. Treatment is daily, supervised in the early phase, and free.

items.title: Take every dose, every day, for the full 6 months
items.description: Never skip. Never stop early — even when you feel completely better after a few weeks. Skipping breeds drug-resistant TB.

items.title: Tell your household and close contacts
items.description: They should all be tested. Children under 5 and pregnant women especially need to be seen quickly. The clinic helps with contact tracing.

items.title: If on HIV treatment — keep both going
items.description: TB and HIV treatments work alongside each other. Tell the clinic about all your medications. Never stop one to make the other easier.

get_help.heading: Where to go
get_help.lede: TB care is one of the most established systems in South African public health. Walk into any clinic — no appointment, no medical aid, no ID required.

helplines.name: Find your nearest clinic
helplines.description: Every government clinic offers free TB testing and treatment
helplines.meta: No appointment · no medical aid required
